content_units: Seasonal Allergy Snapshot
Your brother’s symptoms are most consistent with   allergic rhinitis (hay fever)  , especially because he has:
-   Sneezing
-   Itchy eyes
-   Clear runny nose
-   No fever
-   No facial pain
-   No shortness of breath
This pattern fits allergies more than a cold or sinus infection. Common triggers include   tree, grass, or weed pollen  , dust mites, mold, or pet dander.
Likely Causes and Non-Drowsy OTC Options
Category   What it helps most   Common OTC examples   Notes

Non-drowsy oral antihistamines   Sneezing; itching; runny nose     Cetirizine  ,   loratadine  ,   fexofenadine     Fexofenadine and loratadine are usually least sedating; cetirizine can still cause mild drowsiness in some people

Steroid nasal sprays   Nasal congestion; sneezing; runny nose     Fluticasone  ,   triamcinolone  ,   budesonide     Often the most effective OTC option for ongoing nasal allergy symptoms; may take a few days for full effect
Antihistamine eye drops   Itchy, watery eyes     Ketotifen  ,   olopatadine     Helpful if eye symptoms are prominent
Saline nasal rinse/spray   Irritant/pollen washout; congestion   Saline spray or rinse kits   Drug-free; useful once or twice daily
Decongestants   Stuffy nose     Pseudoephedrine   or   phenylephrine   products   Not ideal for everyone; can raise blood pressure, cause jitteriness, or affect sleep
Combination allergy products   Mixed symptoms   Antihistamine + decongestant products   Can be useful short term, but check stimulant side effects
Practical At-Home Relief Plan
-   Shower and change clothes after being outdoors   to remove pollen.
-   Keep windows closed   during high-pollen days; use air conditioning if possible.
-   Use saline nasal rinse or saline spray   daily to wash out allergens.
-   Apply cool compresses to the eyes   for itching.
-   Avoid rubbing the eyes  , which can worsen irritation.
-   Wash bedding regularly   and consider keeping pets out of the bedroom if pet dander may contribute.
-   Check local pollen levels   and limit outdoor exposure when counts are high.
A practical OTC approach many adults use:
-   A non-drowsy oral antihistamine once daily   for sneezing/itching/runny nose
-   An OTC steroid nasal spray daily   if nasal symptoms persist
-   Antihistamine eye drops   if itchy eyes are a major symptom
When Medical Care Makes More Sense
He should consider seeing a clinician if:
- Symptoms last   more than 2-4 weeks   or keep recurring
- OTC treatment is   not helping enough
- Symptoms are disturbing   sleep, work, or daily function
- He develops possible non-allergy features such as   thick yellow/green mucus  ,   significant facial pain  , or   fever
Red-Flag Symptoms That Warrant Prompt Evaluation
Seek urgent care promptly if he develops:
-   Shortness of breath
-   Wheezing
-   Chest tightness
-   Lip, tongue, or throat swelling
-   Severe rash or hives
-   High fever
-   Severe facial pain
-   Vision changes
-   Symptoms of a severe medication reaction
Context for This Guidance

This is general informational guidance for a   34-year-old adult with mild allergy-type symptoms and no known drug allergies or regular medicines  . OTC labels and pharmacist guidance still matter, especially for decongestants or if he has undiagnosed high blood pressure, glaucoma, prostate/urinary issues, or sleep problems.
